Factual Access States in Diffusion Language Models: From Mechanism to Knowledge Editing and Retrieval

Yuchen Guo ††thanks: This work was done during internship at LIGHTSPEED. Affiliation: The University of Tokyo Email: guo-yuchen027@g.ecc.u-tokyo.ac.jp    Zhuoyuan Mao Affiliation: LIGHTSPEED Email: zhuoyuanmao@global.tencent.com    Yiwen Guo ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Independent Researcher Email: guoyiwen89@gmail.com
Abstract

Factual recall is a lookup: some representation inside the network serves as the key, and what that key is made of decides which queries can retrieve the fact, what an edit must cover, and what a retriever can read. We call it the factual access state. In autoregressive (AR) models the subject position enriches attributes largely independently of the relation, and relation-specific selection happens later, at the readout position. In masked diffusion language models (DLMs) we find the state is assembled differently, and much earlier: in the first attention layer the wording of the relation is routed into the position of whichever entity is visible and the early feed-forward layers look the fact up on this fused representation. The state therefore varies with the relation’s surface form and with the query direction, so the queries about one fact occupy a region of state space rather than a point, and an operation on the fact succeeds only for queries that enter it. We treat the state as an interface to a DLM’s factual knowledge, and put it to two uses. Writing to the state gives a knowledge editor: from one declarative statement, Multi-View Edit fits one shared value per direction across that region and installs it in the early-MLP block, preserving source-prompt reliability while substantially improving paraphrase and reverse question answering, where AR editors gain near zero. Reading it suggests a complementary use: the state at each entity position can serve as a relation-specific retrieval vector with no training, returning both pieces of evidence for two-entity queries on which pooled, prompted and lexical retrievers almost never return both.

Code: https://github.com/Guoyuchen1/dlm-factual-access

1 Introduction

A language model recalls a fact by using an internal representation as a lookup key. We call it the factual access state: its composition determines which queries reach a fact, which states an edit must cover, and what a retriever can read. Knowledge editing changes the value associated with a key (Meng et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2023); evidence retrieval succeeds when query and evidence representations align. Figure 1 previews the mechanism, its contrast with an AR key, and its two uses.

In autoregressive (AR) models, causal masking separates entity access from relation selection. Subject positions accumulate attributes without seeing relation tokens to their right; relation-specific selection occurs later at the final position (Geva et al., 2023; Meng et al., 2022). Locate-then-edit methods therefore update an entity key at the last subject token and recover it from similar prefixes. This is also their limit: the edit is reachable from near-copies of the prefix, but not reliably from paraphrases or reverse questions (Berglund et al., 2023; Kitouni et al., 2024; Yang et al., 2025).

Masked diffusion language models (DLMs) break this premise. They predict any masked subset with bidirectional attention (Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025), so a subject can see relation tokens to its right and an object can become a key in its own direction. Recent work transfers AR edit sites to DLMs and makes edits robust to diffusion decoding (Park and Jo, 2026; Yao et al., 2026). Such ports retain edit-prompt reliability, yet generalise poorly to paraphrases and leave reverse retrieval unchanged. If the key were still the entity alone, these failures would be hard to explain. We therefore ask what representation actually drives lookup (App. A).

Mask-native causal tracing (§2) shows that layer-00 attention routes relation wording into the visible entity; those edges carry 84%84\% of the layer’s causal effect. MLPs 11–88 then retrieve the fact from the fused state. The pipeline replicates in a second DLM and with subject and object roles swapped. The state therefore depends on the entity, the relation’s surface form, and query direction: queries about one fact occupy a region of state space rather than a point. An operation on the fact succeeds only when a query’s state enters that region.

A single-view editor fits one point; Multi-View Edit (§3) instead builds masked forward, reverse, relation, and contextual views, fitting one shared value per direction in the early MLPs. Source-prompt reliability remains at least 97.6%97.6\% on CounterFact and BAKE. On BAKE, reverse question answering rises from 22.4%22.4\% to 63.2%63.2\% on LLaDA-8B and from 20.3%20.3\% to 83.6%83.6\% on Dream-7B, while published AR editors gain under three points. On QAEdit, 32.5%32.5\% and 44.6%44.6\% of previously wrong free-form answers become at least partially correct; unrelated-query activation is unchanged.

To read the state, we use each entity position as a relation-specific retrieval vector (§4). Without training or question decomposition, these vectors retrieve both pieces of evidence for two-entity queries on which a pooled vector usually returns one. Removing the layer-00 relation messages eliminates the advantage.

Our contributions are:

  • •

    Mechanism of factual access states. Causal tracing and attention surgery locate the relation-fused entity state, with replication across two DLMs and both mask directions.

  • •

    Writing to the state: multi-view editing. A shared value per direction covers the statement’s query views; matched-budget ablations and key-space analysis account for the gains.

  • •

    Reading the state: evidence retrieval. Per-entity states retrieve both facts in two-entity queries, with early readout and causal support from relation-routing interventions.

2 How a Masked DLM Accesses a Fact

We first locate factual lookup in LLaDA-8B (§2.2) and show how layer-00 attention assembles the state read by the early MLPs (§2.3). The findings replicate on Dream-7B (App. B.4) and when the object is visible instead of the subject (App. B.5).

2.1 Preliminaries

Masked diffusion language models.

A masked DLM pθp_{\theta} reconstructs randomly hidden tokens. Given xx and a mask rate t∼𝒰⁡(0,1)t\!\sim\!\mathcal{U}(0,1), the corruption operator qtq_{t} replaces each token independently by [MASK] with probability tt, and the model is trained to recover the hidden tokens from the visible ones with bidirectional attention (the masked-diffusion ELBO; App. E.1). Two consequences matter here. Where an AR model exposes only p⁡(o∣s,r)p(o\mid s,r), a masked DLM exposes a whole family of conditionals about the same fact, any subset conditioned on and any subset predicted; this is what §3 exploits. And because the model is queried under qtq_{t} at both training and decoding time, the states it reaches at test time come from partially masked inputs, which is why the tracing below corrupts with [MASK] rather than with noise.

Mask-based causal tracing.

Causal tracing corrupts the input until the answer is lost, then restores internal states one at a time to see which bring it back. We adapt ROME’s formulation (Meng et al., 2022) in two places: next-token prediction becomes masked-position prediction, and Gaussian noise becomes the native [MASK] corruption. For each CounterFact (Meng et al., 2022) triple (s,r,o)(s,r,o) the clean input xcleanx^{\mathrm{clean}} masks the object span, so the task is exactly what the model was trained on, and the corrupted input xcorrx^{\mathrm{corr}} masks both subject and object, removing the cue. Restoring a hidden state hℓ(i)h_{\ell}^{(i)} to its clean value during the corrupted pass defines the indirect effect

IE⁡(ℓ,i)=prest(o∣xcorr,hℓ(i)←hℓclean,(i))−p(o∣xcorr)p⁡(o∣xclean)−p⁡(o∣xcorr),\mathrm{IE}(\ell,i)\;=\;\frac{\,p_{\mathrm{rest}}\!\bigl(o\mid x^{\mathrm{corr}},\;h_{\ell}^{(i)}\!\leftarrow h_{\ell}^{\mathrm{clean},(i)}\bigr)-p\!\bigl(o\mid x^{\mathrm{corr}}\bigr)\,}{\,p\!\bigl(o\mid x^{\mathrm{clean}}\bigr)-p\!\bigl(o\mid x^{\mathrm{corr}}\bigr)\,}, (1)

where IE=1\mathrm{IE}{=}1 means that state alone recovers the clean answer and 00 means it contributes nothing.

2.2 Where the fact is looked up

Restoring a sliding window of w=10w{=}10 adjacent layers (Fig. 2) concentrates the effect almost exclusively on the subject tokens. The profile is bimodal, with an early peak at layers 00–88 and a late peak at 1818–2525, both MLP-dominated. This mirrors a retrieve-then-decode view.

The second peak is an artefact of window stacking. When a single layer is ablated at a time (Fig. 3), only layer-0 attention produces a large effect (IE≈0.23\mathrm{IE}\!\approx\!0.23), while every individual MLP layer contributes ≲0.03\lesssim\!0.03. The late peak is a sum of many small redundant contributions, not a second retrieval site.

What survives is an early block that is jointly, but only jointly, sufficient. Restoring ℓ=0−8\ell{=}0{-}8 reaches IE=0.936\mathrm{IE}{=}0.936, essentially the whole-network ceiling. Layer-00 attention alone (0.2380.238), MLPs 11–88 alone (0.7810.781) and layer-00 MLP alone (−0.015-0.015) each fall short, but layer-00 attention combined with MLPs 11–88 recovers 0.9430.943 (Fig. 5). This is consistent with early-MLP retrieval being conditioned on what layer-00 attention writes into the subject positions, and the block is the site that §3 writes into. App. B adds two further analyses: why the late peak is a serial conduit rather than a second retrieval site, and how the causal locus migrates from subject tokens to the [MASK] readout position.

2.3 Layer 0 assembles the access state

The trace says layer 00 matters but not what it computes. We therefore run five attention-surgery ablations: in each, subject tokens may attend along only one class of edges and all others are zeroed (Table 1).

Letting subject tokens read only from the relation template recovers 84%84\% of the effect, while subject-internal binding, self-attention and the sink are each dispensable. Layer-00 attention thus merges the relation wording into the subject residual stream, producing the relation-sensitive representation that the layer-11–88 MLPs read. We give this representation a name.

Definition 1 (Factual access state).

For a query in which entity ee is visible and the relation is worded as rr, the factual access state a⁡(e,r,d)a(e,r,d) is the residual-stream representation at the position of ee in the early block, after layer-00 attention has routed the wording of rr into it; d∈{fwd,rev}d\in\{\mathrm{fwd},\mathrm{rev}\} records whether ee is the subject or the object of the fact. The early MLPs read it as their input key, k(ℓ)​(⋅,pe)k^{(\ell)}(\cdot,p_{e}) being its image at layer ℓ\ell; §3 writes at k(7)k^{(7)} and §4 reads aa at the output of block 00 or at a deeper layer. Because layer 00 routes the relation into ee, the state is a function of all three arguments,

a=f⁡(e,surface form of ​r,d),a\;=\;f\big(e,\;\text{surface form of }r,\;d\big), (2)

not of the entity alone.

The routing is bidirectional, and so is the state. When the object is kept visible and the subject is hidden instead, the same pipeline runs with the roles swapped: the object position now carries the early-block hidden and MLP effect, its layer-00 attention spikes in the same way, and relation and prefix positions stay flat (App. B.5). The state is therefore formed at whichever entity is visible, with the relation routed into it from either side. Under a causal mask none of this is available: a subject position cannot see a relation to its right, so an autoregressive model keys a fact on the subject and the prefix alone, forms no state on the object side, and cannot express a reverse association natively.

Take-aways.

The factual access state has three properties that guide the rest of the paper. First, it depends on the relation’s surface form, so queries about the same fact occupy a region of state space rather than a point. Second, it forms at whichever entity is visible, enabling both forward and reverse access. Third, it is available from the first block and refined by deeper layers, making early readout possible. These properties motivate the multi-view editing method in §3 and suggest a complementary use for evidence retrieval in §4. The state is also present on fully observed inputs, as confirmed in §4 and App. F.3.

3 Writing to the State: Multi-View Editing from a Single Statement

Multi-View Edit follows §2 on both counts: it leaves attention untouched, since the routing is shared by every query about the fact, and rewrites the early MLPs using a family of masked views covering the access states the same statement induces at test time.

3.1 Method

3.1.1 Editing task and the states an edit must cover

A fact (s,r,o)(s,r,o) is given as a statement xx with spans 𝒮s,𝒮r,𝒮o\mathcal{S}_{s},\mathcal{S}_{r},\mathcal{S}_{o} and a new object o∗o^{*}; the goal is to modify θ\theta so the model behaves as if (s,r,o∗)(s,r,o^{*}) held, leaving unrelated behaviour intact. Following §2, we edit the down-projections Wdown(ℓ)W_{\mathrm{down}}^{(\ell)} of the early block, ℓ∈ℒ={ℓ1,…,ℓL}⊂[1,8]\ell\in\mathcal{L}=\{\ell_{1},\dots,\ell_{L}\}\subset[1,8]. For input uu at position pp, k(ℓ)​(u,p)∈ℝdmlpk^{(\ell)}(u,p)\in\mathbb{R}^{d_{\mathrm{mlp}}} denotes the input to Wdown(ℓ)W_{\mathrm{down}}^{(\ell)}, that is, the representation retrieval reads: the key. Its output z(ℓ)​(u,p)=Wdown(ℓ)​k(ℓ)​(u,p)z^{(\ell)}(u,p)=W_{\mathrm{down}}^{(\ell)}k^{(\ell)}(u,p) is the value. An edit installs one key–value association.

By Definition 1, the key at an entity position is the access state of that query as the layer-ℓ\ell MLP reads it, so it depends on the relation’s surface form and on the query direction, equation 2: an edit fitted to the user’s sentence covers one point in key space, and rephrased or reverse queries activate it weakly. Our design principle is therefore:

Fit the edit to the average of the keys the fact will be queried from, read from either side of it, rather than to the key of the one sentence it happens to be written in.

App. E formalises this principle as expected activation over the fact’s forward and reverse query families and analyses why the view family approximates the desired keys.

3.1.2 View family construction

We construct views with the model’s own corruption operator. Writing ℳ⁡(u,𝒫)\mathcal{M}(u;\mathcal{P}) for the input with tokens at 𝒫\mathcal{P} replaced by [MASK], the forward family hides the object and reads the key at a subject position,

𝒱obj\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{obj}} :ℳ⁡(x,𝒮o),\displaystyle:\;\;\mathcal{M}(x;\mathcal{S}_{o}), supervise ​o∗​ at the masked object span,\displaystyle\text{supervise }o^{*}\text{ at the masked object span,} (3)
𝒱rel​(ρ)\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{rel}}(\rho) :ℳ⁡(x,𝒮o∪ℛρ),ℛρ⊂𝒮r,|ℛρ|=⌈ρ​|𝒮r|⌉,\displaystyle:\;\;\mathcal{M}\big(x;\mathcal{S}_{o}\cup\mathcal{R}_{\rho}\big),\,\mathcal{R}_{\rho}\subset\mathcal{S}_{r},\;|\mathcal{R}_{\rho}|=\lceil\rho\,|\mathcal{S}_{r}|\rceil, relation partly masked, (4)
𝒱ctx\displaystyle\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ctx}} :ℳ⁡(cpre⊕x⊕cpost,𝒮o),\displaystyle:\;\;\mathcal{M}\big(c_{\mathrm{pre}}\oplus x\oplus c_{\mathrm{post}};\,\mathcal{S}_{o}\big), prefix/suffix context templates, (5)

and the reverse family swaps the roles, replacing the object span with the new object and hiding the subject, so the key is read at o∗o^{*}:

𝒱rev:ℳ(x[𝒮o←o∗];𝒮s∪ℛρ),supervise s at the masked subject span,\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{rev}}:\;\;\mathcal{M}\big(x[\mathcal{S}_{o}\!\leftarrow\!o^{*}];\;\mathcal{S}_{s}\cup\mathcal{R}_{\rho}\big),\qquad\text{supervise }s\text{ at the masked subject span,} (6)

For 𝒱rel\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{rel}} and 𝒱rev\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{rev}} we draw nρn_{\rho} occlusion patterns per ratio ρ∈𝒫ρ\rho\in\mathcal{P}_{\rho} (𝒫ρ={0.4,0.7}\mathcal{P}_{\rho}=\{0.4,0.7\}, nρ=3n_{\rho}=3). Whichever span carries the key is never masked. ROME averages the key over a set of prefix templates so that it does not depend on the text around the prompt; 𝒱ctx\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ctx}} does the same. Because a DLM also conditions on what follows the prediction slot, cpostc_{\mathrm{post}} may be non-empty, and we add suffix templates alongside the prefix ones (App. C).

Two axes organise these views, both instantiated by the same qtq_{t}. The direction axis decides how many key–value directions are installed: 𝒱rev\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{rev}} adds the object-side one and, by equation 6, carries relation occlusions on that side too. The masking axis decides how much of each installed direction a reformulated query reaches: 𝒱obj\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{obj}} fixes the association, 𝒱ctx\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ctx}} decorrelates the key from the surrounding discourse, and 𝒱rel\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{rel}} decorrelates it from the relation’s surface form, which by equation 2 is what layer-00 merges in. Together they form a Monte-Carlo sample, restricted to this fact, of the conditionals the model is trained on under qtq_{t}. Setting 𝒫ρ=∅\mathcal{P}_{\rho}=\emptyset leaves 𝒱obj∪𝒱ctx\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{obj}}\cup\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ctx}}. This is the direct port of a locate-then-edit editor, which already averages keys over context templates, and it is the Single-View baseline of Table 2; those two rows therefore isolate 𝒱rel\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{rel}}. Table 15 ablates 𝒱ctx\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ctx}} separately.

3.1.3 One shared value per direction

Let 𝒱=𝒱obj∪𝒱rel∪𝒱ctx\mathcal{V}=\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{obj}}\cup\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{rel}}\cup\mathcal{V}_{\mathrm{ctx}} and ℓ∗=max⁡ℒ\ell^{*}=\max\mathcal{L}. Writing pθ[ℓ∗←z]p_{\theta[\ell^{*}\leftarrow z]} for the model with Wdown(ℓ∗)W_{\mathrm{down}}^{(\ell^{*})}’s output at the key position replaced by zz, we solve

zfwd∗=argminz1|𝒱|∑v∈𝒱wv[−logpθ[ℓ∗←z](o∗|x~v)]+vwd∥z−z0∥2∥z0∥2,∥z−z0∥≤κ∥z0∥,z^{*}_{\mathrm{fwd}}\;=\;\arg\min_{z}\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}w_{v}\Big[-\log p_{\theta[\ell^{*}\leftarrow z]}\big(o^{*}\,\big|\,\tilde{x}_{v}\big)\Big]\;+\;v_{\mathrm{wd}}\,\frac{\lVert z-z_{0}\rVert^{2}}{\lVert z_{0}\rVert^{2}},\qquad\lVert z-z_{0}\rVert\leq\kappa\lVert z_{0}\rVert, (7)

with z0z_{0} the unedited value, wvw_{v} per-view weights (uniform here, since all views are drawn at comparable mask rates), vwdv_{\mathrm{wd}} a relative norm penalty and κ\kappa a clamp. Adam optimises zz alone; model parameters stay frozen. zrev∗z^{*}_{\mathrm{rev}} is obtained the same way over 𝒱rev\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{rev}}, averaging the loss over masked subject positions instead of the object span.

One value is shared across all views of a direction, making equation 7 an intersection rather than a union: one (k,z)(k,z) pair per view would install |𝒱||\mathcal{V}| separate associations, each reachable only from its own point of key space. Instead we ask for a single value that is correct when read out from every key the fact induces. Hard views therefore reshape z∗z^{*} as constraints rather than becoming separate edits, and the installed rank does not grow with |𝒱||\mathcal{V}|.

3.1.4 Keys and the weight update

With pvp_{v} the key position in view vv (a subject position forward, the chosen token of o∗o^{*} in reverse), the key written along is the average over the same views used in equation 7,

kavg=1|𝒱|​∑v∈𝒱k(ℓ)​(x~v,pv),k_{\mathrm{avg}}\;=\;\frac{1}{|\mathcal{V}|}\sum_{v\in\mathcal{V}}k^{(\ell)}\big(\tilde{x}_{v},p_{v}\big), (8)

so that the direction itself is averaged over occlusions and contexts; kavgrevk^{\mathrm{rev}}_{\mathrm{avg}} follows identically over 𝒱rev\mathcal{V}^{\mathrm{rev}}. The update is applied along the whitened direction k^=C−1​kavg/(kavg⊤​C−1​kavg)\hat{k}=C^{-1}k_{\mathrm{avg}}/(k_{\mathrm{avg}}^{\top}C^{-1}k_{\mathrm{avg}}), where CC is the second moment of keys collected from randomly masked inputs under the same qtq_{t} the model traverses during decoding, so that the edit does not fire along directions that are already high-variance across ordinary text (App. C.1; ablated in App. D.4). With ℓi\ell_{i} the ii-th edit layer and m=L−i+1m=L-i+1 the remaining layers, the residual is distributed across ℒ\mathcal{L} as in MEMIT:

Wdown(ℓi)←Wdown(ℓi)+z∗−Wdown(ℓi)​kavgm​k^⊤.W_{\mathrm{down}}^{(\ell_{i})}\;\leftarrow\;W_{\mathrm{down}}^{(\ell_{i})}\;+\;\frac{z^{*}-W_{\mathrm{down}}^{(\ell_{i})}k_{\mathrm{avg}}}{m}\;\hat{k}^{\top}. (9)

Forward and reverse pairs go into the same layers, so one statement installs one forward and one or more reverse directions in one early-MLP block. Attention is never modified: the problem lies in what the state is made of, which the view family addresses, not in the mechanism that assembles it.

3.2 Results

We evaluate on CounterFact (source reliability, paraphrase transfer, neighborhood specificity and locality preservation), BAKE (reverse QA and judgment probes) and QAEdit (free-form answers to natural questions, scored exact, partial or wrong), on LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B. ROME at layer 77 is the base editor, constrained fine-tuning (FT+L) the reproducible DLM baseline, and matched single-view and single-direction variants the controlled comparisons. Benchmark definitions, scoring, configuration and published autoregressive references are in App. D.

3.2.1 CounterFact

Table 2 isolates the relation-masked views against the matched single-view editor. Multi-View keeps source reliability high and consistently improves paraphrase transfer. On LLaDA it also improves neighborhood specificity and locality preservation; on Dream, locality is comparable to Single-View, indicating model-dependent spillover. Locality does not degrade under the wider view family, which agrees with the neighborhood trigger strength of §3.2.4: it is unchanged between the two constructions.

3.2.2 BAKE: Reverse Access

The no-edit row of Table 3 measures the model’s pre-existing preference for the target. Single-Forward edits only the source direction; Single-Binary adds the reverse direction; and Multi-Binary replaces each with the masked view family. BAKE uses a different edit pool from CounterFact. The two axes separate cleanly. Forward-only editing leaves Reverse-QA at the no-edit baseline: bidirectional attention makes the reverse conditional expressible, but a forward update is not reachable from it, so the reverse direction has to be installed explicitly. Once it is, the masking axis governs how much of that direction a reverse query reaches. It adds 21.221.2 points on LLaDA and 10.610.6 on Dream (21.821.8 at a matched view budget, Table 11) and recovers the paraphrase accuracy that Single-Binary gives up. Published autoregressive editors gain under three points on Reverse-QA on GPT-J and LLaMA-2 (App. D.2).

3.2.3 QAEdit: Open-Ended Generation

QAEdit tests the statement-level setting directly: the edit is declarative, whereas evaluation uses an open-ended question and free decoding. For each model and method we evaluate the same 2,2722{,}272 examples that were answered fully wrongly before editing (Table 4). Multi-View gives the strongest source-prompt recovery and question transfer on both models, outperforming FT+L and Single-View on the principal success metrics. The gains are larger on Dream, but free-generation transfer remains incomplete: wrong answers are still the majority on the Gen. split (App. G). The view family also composes with the decoding-state views of Park and Jo (2026): adding them raises the LLaDA-8B weighted score from 0.2500.250 to 0.4300.430 on source prompts and from 0.1870.187 to 0.3520.352 on paraphrased questions (App. D.7).

3.2.4 Edits Fire Where the State Is: A Trigger-Strength Analysis

We compare M1 (one forward key), M2 (forward and reverse keys), and M3 (both directions expanded over the masked view family). For a query key kk, equation 9 gives the trigger strength

α⁡(k)=k^⊤​k=kavg⊤​C−1​kkavg⊤​C−1​kavg,\alpha(k)\;=\;\hat{k}^{\top}k\;=\;\frac{k_{\mathrm{avg}}^{\top}C^{-1}k}{k_{\mathrm{avg}}^{\top}C^{-1}k_{\mathrm{avg}}}, (10)

the fraction of the installed update activated by the query. We report αfire\alpha_{\text{fire}} at its most strongly activated position, alongside the editing effect Δ​logit=log⁡ppost​(onew)−log⁡ppost​(otrue)\Delta\text{logit}=\log p_{\text{post}}(o_{\text{new}})-\log p_{\text{post}}(o_{\text{true}}). On n=1000n{=}1000 BAKE edits with LLaDA-8B and the ROME base editor, Fig. 4 shows that reverse keys strengthen reverse-query activation, while the full view family further improves paraphrase and reverse probes: on Reverse-QA, αfire\alpha_{\text{fire}} rises from 0.080.08 with a forward key alone to 0.560.56 once a reverse key is installed and to 0.610.61 with the full family, while paraphrase activation stays at 0.610.61–0.620.62 throughout and its Δ​logit\Delta\text{logit} more than doubles. On CounterFact neighborhood prompts about other subjects, α=0.03\alpha=0.03 for both single-view and Multi-View edits, well below the queried-fact values. The wider coverage preserves specificity.

4 Reading the State: Evidence Retrieval

4.1 Method

The access state is also an interface to external evidence. We read one retrieval vector per query entity from its state a⁡(e,r,d)a(e,r,d), at the output of block 00 (L0) or at a validation-selected deeper layer. For a token span 𝒮\mathcal{S} in input uu, write its layer-ℓ\ell readout as

v(ℓ)​(u,𝒮)=poolp∈𝒮⁡hℓ(p)​(u).v^{(\ell)}(u,\mathcal{S})=\operatorname{pool}_{p\in\mathcal{S}}h_{\ell}^{(p)}(u). (11)

The pool selects the last entity token at L0 and averages the span at deeper layers. For query qq with entity span 𝒮ei\mathcal{S}_{e_{i}} and evidence card xjx_{j} with subject span 𝒮sj\mathcal{S}_{s_{j}}, we rank cards by

scoreℓ⁡(i,j)=cos⁡(v(ℓ)​(q,𝒮ei),v(ℓ)​(xj,𝒮sj)).\operatorname{score}_{\ell}(i,j)=\cos\!\left(v^{(\ell)}(q,\mathcal{S}_{e_{i}}),v^{(\ell)}(x_{j},\mathcal{S}_{s_{j}})\right). (12)

We fill a shared budget by alternating between the entities’ rankings; no retriever is trained and no query is decomposed. We evaluate on Dream-7B-Instruct and LLaDA-8B-Instruct.

The benchmark is built from PopQA facts (Mallen et al., 2023) and is designed around relations: 5,5285{,}528 evidence cards over five domains and 1919 relations, every entity carrying exactly the four relations of its domain, searched globally for 10,80010{,}800 test queries balanced over the domains and over three layouts, which name one entity, two entities with adjacent entity–relation clauses, or two entities with crossed references (“AA and BB: the director of the former and the composer of the latter”). Single R@1 scores the correct card; dual-target All@2 requires both correct cards within two retrieved cards. A second, entity-conditioned protocol hands every method the same entity-linked candidates, four cards per entity, so that only the relation has to be chosen. Baselines are BM25, whole-query pooling on the same backbones, DiffRetriever’s parallel representative tokens (Wang et al., 2026), and PromptReps on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct (Zhuang et al., 2024). Construction, readout selection and protocols are in App. F.

4.2 Results

Table 5 reports both protocols. On single-entity queries every method retrieves well. On two-entity queries every single-vector method collapses: BM25, pooling, DiffRetriever and PromptReps retrieve both cards for at most 3.06%3.06\% of adjacent and 2.50%2.50\% of crossed queries, because one vector cannot hold two entity–relation bindings. Per-entity access states retrieve both for 38.2838.28–41.94%41.94\% of adjacent and 21.7821.78–38.08%38.08\% of crossed queries from the selected layers. The entity-conditioned protocol, which removes entity coverage as a factor, leaves the ordering unchanged (41.94/38.0841.94/38.08 against at most 16.35/16.2616.35/16.26): the advantage lies in choosing the relation within an entity’s cards, which is what the state binds.

The state is usable as soon as it is formed.

Read after the first block, the access state already retrieves both cards for 24.44%/13.33%24.44\%/13.33\% of adjacent/crossed queries on Dream, and the deeper layers refine it to 38.28/21.7838.28/21.78 (LLaDA: 13.32/9.44→41.94/38.0813.32/9.44\to 41.94/38.08). The readout carries to natural text (App. F.2): on the comparison questions of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA, the first-block readout returns evidence from both gold paragraphs (Both@2) for 41.82%41.82\% and 37.37%37.37\% of questions against 25.15%/26.93%25.15\%/26.93\% for BM25, at 2.62.6 ms per query against 2929–9393 ms for full-depth encoders, and a frozen reader given that evidence gains 44–88 F1 points over the strongest baseline. The early readout is also cheap: reading the state at L0 costs 1.51.5–2.02.0 ms per query on both backbones, against 1313–2626 ms for the full-depth neural retrievers and 265265 ms for PromptReps (Table 5).

The retrieval behaviour is causal.

Subtracting the first attention layer’s relation-token messages at the subject positions drops within-entity relation accuracy to the four-way chance level in all three layouts while entity identification stays at 100%100\%, and substituting the messages of a different relation redirects retrieval toward that relation (App. F.3). Reading the state is thus the counterpart of the write in §3: the layer-00 routing that an edit must cover is what a retrieval vector taken from the state already contains.

5 Conclusion

We asked what a masked DLM computes when it accesses a fact, before asking how to change or use it. Causal tracing reveals a two-stage mechanism: layer-0 attention routes relation wording into the visible entity, and early MLPs look up the fact on the resulting access state. This state depends on the relation’s surface form and query direction, rather than on the entity alone. Writing to this state, Multi-View Edit fits shared values across multiple query views, improving paraphrase and reverse generalisation while preserving source-prompt reliability and locality. Reading it provides a complementary insight: per-entity access states can serve as relation-specific retrieval vectors. Our experiments offer a proof of concept for using these states to access external evidence, connecting knowledge editing and retrieval through a shared mechanism of factual access. Two limitations bound these claims. The editor assumes identifiable subject, relation and object spans, which CounterFact and BAKE supply but arbitrary user statements may not, and free-generation transfer on QAEdit remains incomplete, since wrong answers are still the majority on paraphrased questions (App. G).

AI Use Statement

Generative AI models were used as experimental components, as described in the paper. AI-assisted tools were otherwise used only for limited language polishing and code troubleshooting. All methodological decisions, experimental results, interpretations, and final manuscript content were reviewed and approved by the authors, who take full responsibility for this work.

Reproducibility Statement

The paper specifies the mask-native causal tracing protocol, multi-view editing procedure, and per-entity retrieval readouts. Appendix B reports additional mechanism and role-reversal checks. Appendix C records editing hyperparameters, context templates, seed, precision, and compute, while Appendix C.1 details covariance estimation under the DLM masking distribution. Appendix D documents editing benchmarks, baselines, and ablations. Appendix F specifies corpus construction, validation and test splits, readout selection, scoring, and evaluation protocols for both controlled and natural retrieval settings. Seed 4242 fixes sampled masks and covariance estimation; the editor uses no random initialisation or stochastic retraining. Code is available at https://github.com/Guoyuchen1/dlm-factual-access.

Ethics Statement

Knowledge editing can be misused to make false claims accessible through multiple phrasings and query directions. Our experiments use controlled factual-edit benchmarks and report locality and neighborhood specificity to assess unintended changes; these results do not establish safety for deployment. The retrieval experiments use public benchmark corpora and may inherit errors or biases in their source material. We collected no private user data and conducted no human-subject experiments.

Appendix A Detailed Related Work

A.1 Knowledge editing in autoregressive language models

Knowledge editing aims to change selected model behaviour while preserving unrelated predictions. Existing approaches include constrained fine-tuning and learned editors (Zhu et al., 2020; De Cao et al., 2021; Mitchell et al., 2022a), direct parameter rewriting (Meng et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2023; Li et al., 2024; Fang et al., 2025), and external or semi-external memories designed for scalable and lifelong updates (Mitchell et al., 2022b; Zheng et al., 2023; Hartvigsen et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2024). The locate-then-edit family is closest to our work. ROME models an MLP as a key–value memory and installs one association with a rank-one update; MEMIT distributes related updates across several layers. Later methods refine the edited subspace or update rule, but retain the AR factorisation in which a subject-side representation is read from a prefix and the target is predicted to its right.

This literature has traditionally evaluated three properties: reliability on the source prompt, generalisation to paraphrases, and locality on unrelated prompts. More recent benchmarks expose dimensions not captured by this triad. MQuAKE and RippleEdits test whether a local change propagates to related or multi-hop consequences (Zhong et al., 2023; Cohen et al., 2024); QAEdit shows that edited-prompt success can degrade under natural questions, free-form decoding, and sequential editing (Yang et al., 2025). Our experiments therefore include both conventional forced-choice scores and open-ended statement-to-question transfer.

A.2 From prompt editing to statement-level editing

Most locate-then-edit methods receive a natural-language statement but reduce it to one directional conditional. For a fact (s,r,o)(s,r,o), an AR editor typically optimises the association queried by p⁡(o∣s,r)p(o\mid s,r). This is sufficient for the source continuation, but it is not equivalent to making the model use the statement as knowledge. The same proposition may be queried by masking the object, recovering the subject from (r,o)(r,o), judging whether the proposition is true, omitting part of the relation, or embedding it in a question and generating an answer. Under left-to-right attention, several of these conditionals cannot be formed from the same token order because the desired target appears before some of its evidence.

Our use of statement-level editing refers to this distinction. The user still supplies one declarative edit, not a hand-written set of questions or paraphrases. The editor then uses the DLM’s native corruption operator to derive multiple conditional views of that statement. This differs from ordinary prompt augmentation in two ways. First, the views include different prediction directions, not only surface rewrites of the same forward prompt. Second, they are generated from the model’s masking distribution rather than from the evaluation benchmark’s paraphrase set. Consequently, success on a held-out question or reverse probe tests whether the installed association is reachable from a new conditional view, rather than whether the exact evaluation prompt was used during editing.

This framing should not be read as claiming that one forward update automatically induces all reverse knowledge. Our BAKE ablation shows the opposite: bidirectional attention makes an object-side conditional expressible, but most reverse gains arise only after the reverse direction is explicitly included in the edit group. The contribution is that both directions, relation occlusions, and contextual variants can be derived from one statement and installed in a common early-MLP block.

A.3 Reversal, bidirectional knowledge, and model editing

The reversal curse describes the failure of AR models trained on “AA is BB” to reliably answer the inverse query “BB is AA” (Berglund et al., 2023). The factorisation account attributes this failure to which tokens are predicted from which contexts during language modelling (Kitouni et al., 2024). BAKE transfers the issue from training to model editing: an editor may successfully change the forward association while leaving reverse retrieval unchanged. BIRD introduces bidirectional objectives within the AR setting (Ma et al., 2023), but AR token order still constrains which conditionals can be represented as ordinary target-final prompts.

Masked DLMs reconstruct arbitrary masked subsets and therefore weaken this structural asymmetry (Sahoo et al., 2024; Nie et al., 2025; Ye et al., 2025). Recent analyses nevertheless find that bidirectional attention does not eliminate reversal failures; proposed explanations include entity fragmentation, asymmetry in data or relations, and the degree to which forward and reverse queries share representations (He et al., 2026; Jeon et al., 2026). These findings motivate our separation between availability and reachability: a reverse conditional can exist in the architecture while a parameter update fitted to one key still fails to activate from the reverse query. Multi-View Edit addresses reachability by constructing and installing keys from both sides of the same statement.

A.4 Knowledge editing in masked diffusion language models

Concurrent work has established that factual associations can be edited in masked diffusion language models. Park and Jo (2026) transfer locate-then-edit to masked DLMs and show that the edit site carries over from the AR setting: causal tracing highlights an early-to-mid-layer MLP at the last subject token, and editing is most effective there. They then identify a failure mode specific to diffusion decoding: a value fitted on a fully masked target degrades once some target tokens have been revealed, because the edit was never optimised for those intermediate states. They correct it by exposing partially unmasked target states during value optimisation. TimeROME-DLM instead combines temporal causal tracing with a low-rank residual memory applied at inference time, leaving the backbone parameters unchanged (Yao et al., 2026).

Two orthogonal failure modes.

We take the localisation of Park and Jo (2026) as given and ask a different question about the same site: what the retrieval step there actually reads. The two diagnoses concern different axes of the same editor. Theirs is about the decoding trajectory: a value optimised on one masking state of the target is not optimised for the intermediate states traversed while that target is generated. Ours is about the query entrance: a value optimised at one key is only weakly activated when the relation is reworded or the query is posed from the object side (equation 2). Neither subsumes the other, and they compose: in the notation of §3.1.2 their correction is a further view type supervised on the same shared value, a partial reveal of 𝒮o\mathcal{S}_{o} rather than an occlusion of 𝒮r\mathcal{S}_{r}. App. D.7 carries this composition out on QAEdit and confirms it: adding their partial-reveal views to our view family raises the weighted score on LLaDA-8B from 0.2500.250 to 0.4300.430 on source prompts and from 0.1870.187 to 0.3520.352 on paraphrased questions, and largely removes the multi-token degradation of App. D.6. Their method is therefore complementary to ours rather than a competing one.

Why no concurrent DLM editor appears in Table 3.

The reason is structural rather than empirical. Both concurrent methods supervise a forward conditional in which the subject stays visible and the key is read on the subject side; neither installs an object-side association, so neither can make a forward edit reachable from a reverse query, which is the quantity the reverse columns of Table 3 measure. The Single-Forward rows already bound what any forward-only construction achieves there. TimeROME-DLM is further removed, since it leaves the backbone unchanged and edits through an inference-time residual memory, which is not commensurable with a key-coverage account of a weight update. We therefore use constrained fine-tuning (FT+L) as a reproducible masked-DLM baseline and, more importantly, compare Multi-View Edit against matched single-view and single-direction variants that isolate the contribution of each proposed design axis. Published AR results are collected in App. D.2 as scale references rather than controlled comparisons.

A.5 Reading language-model representations for retrieval

Dense retrieval encodes a query and a passage into one vector each and ranks by inner product (Karpukhin et al., 2020); late-interaction models keep one vector per token and score with MaxSim (Khattab and Zaharia, 2020); BM25 ranks by lexical overlap (Robertson and Zaragoza, 2009). A second line uses a frozen language model as the encoder. PromptReps prompts an autoregressive LM to emit representative tokens whose hidden states serve as dense and sparse representations (Zhuang et al., 2024); LLM2Vec and Echo embeddings obtain a pooled representation from a decoder by enabling bidirectional attention or repeating the input (BehnamGhader et al., 2024; Springer et al., 2025); DiffRetriever carries the representative-token recipe to masked diffusion LMs, appending mask positions to query and passage and encoding them in parallel (Wang et al., 2026). In all of these the query becomes one vector, or a small set of vectors placed by a prompt, rather than a representation read from the model’s own processing of the entities the query mentions. Entity-centric questions are a known weak point of pooled dense retrievers (Sciavolino et al., 2021), and PopQA, from which our evidence corpus is built, isolates the long-tail entity facts on which retrieval augmentation is most needed (Mallen et al., 2023). Questions that ask about several entities, such as the comparison questions of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA (Yang et al., 2018; Ho et al., 2020), are usually handled upstream, by decomposing the question into sub-questions before retrieval (Press et al., 2023; Khot et al., 2023) or by entity linking followed by per-entity retrieval.

Our retriever differs on both counts. It reads representations the model already computes, the access state at each entity position, so the per-entity, relation-bound query vectors that decomposition methods construct externally are obtained from the contextualised entity positions of the query itself, with no retriever training, no prompt-placed representative tokens and no parser. Because the state is present from the first block on (§2), the query encoder can read it early, and because the same state is what the early MLPs read for parametric lookup, the retrieval readout and the editing write of §3 operate on one representation. Benchmarks, protocols and controls are reported in App. F.

Appendix B Additional Mechanism Analyses

This appendix reports five auxiliary causal-tracing analyses that complement §2. The first three characterise the retrieval pipeline on LLaDA-8B in more detail and justify claims made in passing in the main text: (i) the early peak is dominated by MLP rather than attention (App. B.1), (ii) the two visual “peaks” are arranged in a strict retrieve-then-decode series, not in parallel (App. B.2), and (iii) the causal locus migrates from subject tokens to the [MASK] position only in the last few layers (App. B.3). The last two establish that the pipeline is not an artefact of one checkpoint or one mask layout: it replicates on Dream-7B (App. B.4) and runs role-swapped when the subject rather than the object is masked (App. B.5), which is the property that Definition 1 and the reverse views of §3 rely on. Unless otherwise stated, all numbers are on CounterFact with LLaDA-8B and follow the tracing protocol of §2.1.

B.1 Selective Peak Ablation & Channel Decomposition

We compare four restoration policies applied to subject tokens under the mask-corruption protocol of §2.1: Early Only (restore layers 00–88), Late Only (restore layers 1818–2525), Both Peaks (restore both windows), and All Layers (restore the entire stack). For each policy we further split the restored signal by channel into Full Block, Attention Only, and FF/MLP Only (Fig. 6, n=550n{=}550).

Findings.

Three observations follow directly from Fig. 6. First, on the Full Block the four policies are nearly indistinguishable (0.9460.946–1.0121.012), which by itself would suggest that either peak is sufficient. Second, this appearance is entirely carried by MLPs: the MLP-only panel shows Early Only =0.917=0.917 compared with Late Only =0.207=0.207, a ∼4.4×\sim 4.4\times gap. Third, the attention channel is uniformly weak (all four conditions ≤0.389\leq 0.389), consistent with the single-layer analysis in §2.2 that attributes essentially all attention-side causal mass to layer 00.

B.2 Cross-Peak Patching: Are the Two Peaks in Series or in Parallel?

Sec. B.1 shows that either peak, restored alone on the Full Block, produces near-ceiling IE. This is compatible with two very different mechanisms: the peaks could be redundant parallel channels (each independently reconstructs the answer), or a serial pipeline (the late peak only works because the early peak feeds it). We disambiguate by conditional patching: we restore one peak while simultaneously blocking the other, i.e. pinning the blocked peak’s hidden states to their corrupted values so that no information can flow through it.

Findings.

The asymmetry in Fig. 7 is striking:

  • •

    Late Only =1.012=1.012 and Late ++ Block Early =1.012=1.012 (Full Block): blocking the early peak leaves the late peak’s performance untouched, because when we restore the late peak we hand it a clean representation directly.

  • •

    Early Only =0.946=0.946 but Early ++ Block Late =0.019=0.019: restoring the early peak alone is useless if the late peak is blocked, because the recovered representation cannot reach the readout.

The MLP channel shows the same pattern with an even larger gap (0.917→0.1480.917\to 0.148).

Take-away.

The two peaks are serially composed, not parallel. The early peak is the source of the fact-relevant signal; the late peak is a downstream conduit that carries the already-retrieved representation toward the [MASK] readout. This is exactly what one expects from the retrieve-then-decode view articulated in §2.2.

B.3 Subject-to-[MASK] Handoff: Mirror Analysis on the Readout Position

The analyses so far restore hidden states at subject tokens. To see how and when the signal migrates to the position that actually emits the prediction, we run a mirror experiment (Exp 7) that keeps the tracing protocol identical to Exp 3 (§2.2) but restores hidden states at the [MASK] position instead of at the subject range. Fig. 8 overlays the two curves.

Findings.

Reading Fig. 8 from left to right along the layer axis gives a four-stage picture of fact recall in a masked DLM:

  1. 1.

    Layer ∼0\sim\!0: subject-side anchoring by attention. The attention panel shows a single dominant spike at layer 00 on the subject curve (≈0.23\approx\!0.23), with the [MASK] curve near zero. This is the context-fusion step characterised in §2.3.

  2. 2.

    Layers ∼1\sim\!1–2424: subject-side persistence and processing. On the Full Block the subject curve stays in [0.7,0.9][0.7,0.9] while the [MASK] curve remains near zero, indicating that the fact-relevant representation continues to live at the subject positions throughout most of the network.

  3. 3.

    Layers ∼25\sim\!25–2828: subject →\to [MASK] handoff. The two curves cross: the subject curve drops sharply while the [MASK] curve rises. Bidirectional attention allows this transfer to happen in a narrow band rather than being smeared across many layers.

  4. 4.

    Top layers: [MASK]-side local readout. In the last few layers the [MASK] curve dominates (Full Block →1.0\to 1.0; attention ≈0.12\approx\!0.12; MLP peaks around layer 2727). The final decoding is performed locally at the readout position, after the retrieved representation has been delivered there.

B.4 Cross-Model Robustness: Dream-7B Reproduces the LLaDA Pipeline

We rerun the 1-D causal trace of §2.1 on Dream-7B, an independently trained masked DLM whose architecture, training data and mask schedule differ from LLaDA-8B. For each fact we compute the average indirect effect AIE⁡(ℓ,τ)\mathrm{AIE}(\ell,\tau) separately at each layer ℓ\ell and each role-typed position τ∈{Subject,Relation,Prefix,[MASK]}\tau\in\{\text{Subject},\text{Relation},\text{Prefix},\text{[MASK]}\}.

Findings.

Fig. 9 matches the LLaDA fingerprint on every axis we tested:

  1. 1.

    Low-layer subject-side attention dominates. On the attention panel, the Subject curve reaches AIE≈0.25\mathrm{AIE}\!\approx\!0.25 at layers 00–55 and then collapses to near zero from layer 66 onwards, mirroring the single-layer-00 dominance we established on LLaDA (§2.2).

  2. 2.

    Subject-anchored bimodal footprint on Hidden / MLP. The Subject curve on Hidden states peaks around layer 55 and remains elevated up to layer ∼20\sim\!20; the MLP panel shows the same subject-side elevation over the early block.

  3. 3.

    Relation-side second peak in the top block. An attention-side Relation peak appears at layers 1818–2323 (AIE≈0.20\mathrm{AIE}\!\approx\!0.20), consistent with the subject→\toreadout handoff band identified on LLaDA (App. B.3).

  4. 4.

    [MASK]-side local readout. The [MASK] curve stays near zero for most of the network and rises only in the last few layers, exactly as observed for LLaDA.

Because Dream-7B shares neither pretraining data nor exact model shape with LLaDA-8B yet reproduces all four features, the “low-layer context fusion ++ early-MLP lookup” pipeline appears to be shared across the two masked DLMs studied rather than specific to the LLaDA checkpoint. This is the mechanistic version of the empirical cross-model transfer already reported in §3.2, and it is what makes it safe to apply the same Multi-View recipe unchanged across the two DLMs. It does not by itself explain why the editor’s quantitative gains differ so much between the two checkpoints (App. G).

B.5 Cross-Layout Robustness: The Mechanism Survives a Subject-Side Mask

The tracing setup in §2.1 always masks the object span at the tail of the prompt. This raises a legitimate concern that the pipeline we characterise is specific to tail-side prediction, and that observed “fact retrieval” merely reflects how DLMs handle their canonical next-mask completion. To rule this out we construct a subject-side variant in which we keep the object visible and instead mask the subject span in the middle of the prompt (denoted [MASK_subj]). We then re-run the 1-D causal trace at each role-typed position, using LLaDA-8B as the reference model.

Findings.

Compared with the tail-mask setting, Fig. 10 shows that the shape of the pipeline is preserved and that only the token roles rotate to their new positions:

  1. 1.

    The Object position now inherits the role previously played by the subject: Hidden AIE rises above 0.90.9 in the early block, MLP AIE peaks around 0.90.9 in layers 00–88, and the Attention channel spikes to ∼0.45\sim\!0.45 at layer 00, the same low-layer context-fusion signature reported for the subject side.

  2. 2.

    The [MASK_subj] position (mid-sentence) takes over in the top layers on all three channels: Hidden and Attention AIE≈0.5\mathrm{AIE}\!\approx\!0.5 at the last layer, and MLP ≈0.25\approx\!0.25, mirroring the [MASK]-side readout of App. B.3.

  3. 3.

    Relation and Prefix positions remain flat throughout, i.e. they still do not carry fact-specific causal mass, regardless of whether they precede or follow the masked span.

This is precisely the property that legitimises the bidirectional access state of Definition 1. When we build a reverse key by masking the subject and keeping the object visible, we are not constructing an out-of-distribution probe; we are exercising the same pipeline in a role-swapped configuration that the model already supports natively. It is also, in our view, the mechanistic reason why Binary / bidirectional editing is a well-defined operation on a masked DLM but not on an autoregressive one: only in the DLM does the subject position causally depend on tokens that appear to its right. Combined with the cross-model replication of App. B.4, the pipeline used by Multi-View Edit is thus doubly robust: it survives a change of model (LLaDA-8B ↔\leftrightarrow Dream-7B) and a change of mask layout (object-side ↔\leftrightarrow subject-side), which justifies treating the forward and reverse keys as symmetric, first-class ingredients of a single editing rule.

Appendix C Editor Implementation Details

Table 7 lists all hyperparameters shared across LLaDA-8B and Dream-7B, and Table 8 enumerates the context templates used for z∗z^{*} optimisation and key extraction.

C.1 Covariance estimation under the masking distribution

The update of equation 9 is written along k^=C−1​kavg/(kavg⊤​C−1​kavg)\hat{k}=C^{-1}k_{\mathrm{avg}}/(k_{\mathrm{avg}}^{\top}C^{-1}k_{\mathrm{avg}}), with

C=𝔼x∼𝒟𝔼t∼𝒰⁡(0.15,0.75)𝔼x~∼qt(⋅∣x)[k(ℓ)(x~,⋅)k(ℓ)(x~,⋅)⊤],C\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{\,x\sim\mathcal{D}}\;\mathbb{E}_{\,t\sim\mathcal{U}(0.15,0.75)}\;\mathbb{E}_{\,\tilde{x}\sim q_{t}(\cdot\mid x)}\Big[k^{(\ell)}(\tilde{x},\cdot)\,k^{(\ell)}(\tilde{x},\cdot)^{\top}\Big], (13)

estimated offline on a corpus sample 𝒟\mathcal{D}. Rescaling by the second moment of keys the model actually produces suppresses directions that are already high-variance across ordinary text, so that the edit does not fire on unrelated inputs. The DLM-specific choice is the second expectation: keys are collected from randomly masked inputs, drawn from the same qtq_{t} the model traverses during decoding, not from clean text, so the statistics mirror what the view family of §3.1.2 does in the supervision. Concretely, we estimate the key covariance at each edit layer as C^ℓ=𝔼⁡[kℓ(i)​kℓ(i)⊤∣i∉M]\hat{C}_{\ell}=\mathbb{E}[\,k_{\ell}^{(i)}{k_{\ell}^{(i)}}^{\top}\mid i\notin M\,], where the expectation marginalises over the DLM’s mask-ratio schedule and the conditioning i∉Mi\notin M restricts to unmasked (content) positions, matching the distribution of keys seen during actual editing. The inputs are masked; it is the positions at which keys are read that are restricted to unmasked tokens. We invert with Tikhonov regularisation: C^ℓ−1←(C^ℓ+λ​I)−1\hat{C}_{\ell}^{-1}\leftarrow(\hat{C}_{\ell}+\lambda I)^{-1}. App. D.4 isolates the choice: relative to clean-text covariance, estimating the statistics under qtq_{t} adds 2.62.6 pp of paraphrase transfer and improves neighborhood specificity and locality monotonically, while reliability is unaffected. The covariance is estimated once per model on WikiText-103 (Table 7) and cached.

C.2 Reproducibility

The editor involves no random initialisation or stochastic retraining. Seed 4242 fixes sampled masking patterns and covariance estimation. Each run fits in a single GPU with approximately 50,00050{,}000 MiB of memory, which is the peak observed for LLaDA-8B with the largest view family; covariance estimation is performed once per model and cached. We will release the full editing and evaluation code, together with the cached covariance statistics and the view-construction scripts, upon acceptance.

Appendix D Editing Experiments: Details and Additional Results

D.1 Benchmarks, scoring, and configuration

Models and benchmarks.

CounterFact measures source reliability, paraphrase transfer, neighborhood specificity and locality preservation; BAKE adds reverse QA and judgment probes (Meng et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2023); QAEdit supplies declarative edits and scores freely generated answers to natural questions as exact (11), partial (0.50.5) or wrong (00) (Yang et al., 2025). Neighborhood (Neigh.) scores interference on similar subjects. Locality preservation (Loc-Pres.) is the fraction of unrelated prompts on which the edited model’s top-ranked continuation is unchanged from the pre-edit model, so it scores interference on unrelated text.

Scoring.

CounterFact and BAKE follow the ROME forced-choice criterion: onewo_{\mathrm{new}} must outrank otrueo_{\mathrm{true}} (or Yes must outrank No). For QAEdit we report score-bucket frequencies and s=(n1.0+0.5​n0.5)/ns=(n_{1.0}+0.5n_{0.5})/n. We retain only examples the base model answers fully wrongly (pre<0.5\texttt{pre}<0.5), so every non-zero score is attributable to the edit.

Editor configuration.

Multi-View changes key/value construction and can use a standard weight-update rule underneath. Main results use ROME at layer 77, written at the last subject token; App. D.3 reports the position sweep. MEMIT spreads the same construction over layers 55–77, all within the mechanistic block. Concurrent DLM editors address a different failure mode and install no object-side key, so they are not comparable on the reverse probes of §3.2.2 (App. A). On QAEdit, where their correction does apply, we reproduce one of them and compose it with ours (App. D.7). We include constrained fine-tuning (FT+L) as a reproducible DLM baseline and show published AR results only as scale references (App. D.2). Hyperparameters are listed in App. C.

D.2 Published autoregressive references

Tables 2 and 3 compare Multi-View Edit against matched single-view and single-direction variants and against constrained fine-tuning on the same DLMs. Published results for autoregressive editors on GPT-J (6B) and LLaMA-2 (7B), reproduced from the original papers (Meng et al., 2022; Meng et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2023), are collected in Table 9 as scale references: they concern different models and different edit pools, so they are not controlled comparisons. On the reverse probes they show the pattern the main text refers to: Reverse-QA gains of at most 2.92.9 points from a forward edit. The AR Reverse-Judge deltas should be read as upper bounds, because BAKE reports a pre-edit floor of zero that is inherited from the QA probe rather than measured on the judgment probe (see below).

The pre-edit floor of BAKE’s judgment probe.

BAKE reports a pre-edit score of zero on both reverse probes for every base LLM, attributing this to the filtering of edits whose reverse fact the model already holds. The filter, however, is defined only in the QA direction: given o∗o^{*} and r−1r^{-1}, an edit is retained if the base model prefers s∗s^{*} over ss, which is exactly the RQS criterion P⁡(s)>P⁡(s∗)P(s)>P(s^{*}). RJS scores a different quantity, P⁡(yes)>P⁡(no)P(\text{yes})>P(\text{no}) on a judgment prompt, and nothing in the filter constrains it. A model that has been filtered to not prefer ss in the QA direction may still answer yes to “Whether the capital of England is Paris?”, through acquiescence bias, through sensitivity to the surface form of the question, or simply because the judgment prompt makes the target explicit rather than requiring it to be generated. The zero is thus inherited from the QA probe rather than measured on the judgment probe.

Two consequences. First, the AR Δ\Delta on R-Judge should be read as an upper bound: whatever fraction of judgment prompts the unedited model already answers affirmatively is being credited to the editor. Second, this asymmetry works against the DLMs in a naive reading of Table 3, since our pre-edit rows are measured rather than assumed (30.6%30.6\% on LLaDA-8B and 18.2%18.2\% on Dream-7B) and are subtracted in full. That these measured floors are far from zero on the same style of prompt is itself the clearest evidence that a judgment probe carries a non-trivial affirmative baseline. Directly measuring the AR judgment floor on the released BAKE prompts would settle the question and is a straightforward addition we did not have the compute budget to include.

D.3 Which subject position should the edit be written at?

Why the question is different in a DLM.

Locate-then-edit methods developed for AR models write the update at the last subject token. This convention is a consequence of the causal mask: under left-to-right attention, an earlier subject token has not yet seen the remainder of the subject span, and no subject token can see the relation template placed to its right, so the last subject position is the only one whose residual stream carries the complete (s,r)(s,r) context by the time the early MLPs read it. The choice is therefore forced rather than empirical.

Section 2 shows that this argument does not carry over. Layer-00 attention in a masked DLM fuses the relation template into the subject residual stream (Table 1), and because attention is bidirectional it does so at every subject position simultaneously: each subject token attends to the full relation span regardless of its index within the span. The (s,r)(s,r)-conditioned key of equation 2 is thus available at any position inside 𝒮s\mathcal{S}_{s}, and which one we write the rank-one update at becomes an empirical choice rather than a structural constraint.

Selection protocol.

Because the position is not fixed by the architecture and the design space is small, we settle it empirically, but we separate selection from reporting. The sweep is run on a development pool of n=4694n{=}4694 BAKE edits (Table 10, top block), the winning setting is fixed, and it is then re-evaluated once on a disjoint held-out split of n=1000n{=}1000 edits that is used for no other tuning decision in this paper (Table 10, bottom block). The held-out split reproduces the development ranking exactly: last is best on all four columns on both splits, and the full three-way ordering is identical column by column (last >> mean >> first on Reliability and Paraphrase, last >> first >> mean on both reverse probes). The Paraphrase advantage of last shrinks from 17.117.1 to 14.514.5 pp under held-out evaluation, i.e. some but not all of it was selection effect.

Findings.

On the held-out split, three of the four columns are largely insensitive to where in the subject span the update is written: Reliability varies by 0.70.7 pp, Reverse-QA by 2.42.4 pp and Reverse-Judge by 1.91.9 pp across the three settings, differences that are small relative to the effect of the design axes in §3.2.2. This is what §2.3 predicts, and it is the sense in which our result is not a recovery of the AR convention: that convention rests on the last subject token being the only position with a usable key, whereas here first and mean both remain serviceable (≥97.5%\geq 97.5\% Reliability, ≥58.6%\geq 58.6\% R-QA), i.e. every subject position carries a usable (s,r)(s,r)-conditioned key.

Paraphrase is the exception, ranging over 67.6%67.6\%–82.1%82.1\%: a 14.514.5 pp spread on held-out data, comparable to the effect of the view family itself. The write position therefore deserves treatment as a first-class design axis rather than an implementation detail. We read the Paraphrase gap as a quantitative effect layered on top of the layer-00 mechanism rather than a structural one: positions later in the subject span aggregate more of the surrounding context into the key even though all positions can access it, so an update written there is triggered by a slightly broader region of key space.

D.4 Ablations

Matched view budget.

Multi-View supervises the shared value over more views than Single-View does, so its gains could in principle come from the extra optimisation signal rather than from the relation-masked views themselves. We therefore construct a budget-matched variant, Multi-Binary (matched), that keeps the relation-masked and reverse construction but removes six views from the context family, leaving it with the same number of views as Single-Binary. Any remaining gap is then attributable to which views are used, not how many. Tables 11 and 12 report this comparison on BAKE and CounterFact; all other components of the editor, including the base editor, the write position, and the number of optimisation steps, are held fixed.

Findings.

At a matched budget of 1414 views, the relation-masked construction already recovers almost all of the gain. On BAKE it lifts Paraphrase from 65.5%65.5\% to 82.2%82.2\% and Reverse-QA from 42.0%42.0\% to 63.8%63.8\%, against 84.6%84.6\% and 63.2%63.2\% for the full 2020-view configuration; on Reverse-QA the matched variant is in fact marginally ahead. CounterFact shows the same pattern, with the matched variant within 1.11.1 pp of the full configuration on Paraphrase (66.9%66.9\% vs. 67.9%67.9\%) and within 2.72.7 and 0.30.3 pp on Neighborhood and Loc-Pres. The gains of Multi-View therefore come from which views the shared value is supervised on rather than from how many: adding six further context views on top of the relation-masked family buys a further 2.32.3 pp of Paraphrase on BAKE and little elsewhere. Since the number of installed directions is fixed by construction (§3.1.3), this also rules out the alternative explanation that the improvement merely reflects more values being written into the weights.

KL locality regularisation.

Table 13 moves the KL comparison out of the main results. Overall, KL has little influence on the result: on LLaDA-8B all changes are within 1.61.6 percentage points, while on Dream-7B its modest locality gains (0.90.9–1.91.9 points) are offset by lower reliability and paraphrase accuracy. We therefore use the simpler unregularised objective as the default.

Whitening covariance.

equation 13 estimates covariance from randomly masked inputs so that whitening matches the DLM deployment distribution. Table 14 isolates that choice against clean-text covariance and against no whitening at all, holding the model, base editor, data split and every non-covariance hyperparameter fixed.

Findings.

Reliability is essentially unaffected by the choice of statistics (97.2%97.2\%–98.1%98.1\%): whitening does not determine whether the association is installed. It determines how well the installed direction generalises and how much it leaks. Moving from no whitening to clean-text covariance recovers 5.85.8 pp of Paraphrase, and estimating the covariance under the model’s own masking distribution adds a further 2.62.6 pp; Neighborhood and Loc-Pres. improve monotonically in the same order (70.9%→72.9%→73.7%70.9\%\to 72.9\%\to 73.7\% and 83.4%→88.0%→89.9%83.4\%\to 88.0\%\to 89.9\%). The gap between the two whitened rows is the part attributable to equation 13 specifically, and it is consistent with the motivation given there: the keys an edit is actually queried from at decoding time are drawn from qtq_{t}, not from clean text, so second-order statistics collected under qtq_{t} describe the deployment geometry more accurately.

Prefix and suffix contexts.

Because a DLM conditions bidirectionally, contextual templates can be placed before or after the masked prediction span. Table 15 compares three configurations on CounterFact: no contextual templates, prefix-only templates, and the full prefix-plus-suffix family. All other components of the editor are held fixed.

Findings.

Contextual views substantially improve edit success and generalisation on both models. Relative to using no context templates, prefix-plus-suffix supervision raises Reliability by 6.56.5 percentage points and Paraphrase by 29.729.7 points on LLaDA-8B; the corresponding gains on Dream-7B are 15.215.2 and 31.031.0 points. Adding suffix templates on top of prefix-only supervision accounts for a substantial share of the paraphrase gain on both models (+18.5+18.5 points on LLaDA-8B and +13.8+13.8 on Dream-7B), confirming that the extra conditioning direction available to a bidirectional model is not redundant with prefix context. These improvements come with modest locality costs: compared with no contextual templates, Neighborhood decreases by 2.4/3.42.4/3.4 points and Loc-Pres. by 2.6/2.22.6/2.2 points on LLaDA/Dream. Overall, bidirectional prefix-plus-suffix conditioning offers a favourable trade-off, producing large gains in reliability and paraphrase transfer for a relatively small reduction in locality.

D.5 Stability under sequential editing

We additionally evaluate whether the edits remain stable when multiple facts are installed sequentially. Starting from the same base model, we apply ROME updates one at a time without restoring the original weights, and evaluate the cumulatively edited model after up to T=100T=100 edits. We compare Single-Binary with Multi-Binary under the same editing protocol.

Findings.

Reliability is unaffected by accumulation: both methods stay at 100%100\% through T=25T=25 and at ≈99%\approx 99\% after 100100 sequential edits, so previously installed associations are not overwritten by later ones. Generalisation and locality both take their largest hit between T=1T=1 and T=10T=10 and then plateau or partly recover, and all three metrics remain well above the 0.50.5 reference line at every TT. On generalisation the two constructions separate: Multi-Binary drops to 80%80\% at T=10T=10 against 70%70\% for Single-Binary, the two coincide at 86%86\% at T=25T=25, and thereafter Multi-Binary holds 86%86\% at T=50T=50 and 89.5%89.5\% at T=100T=100 while Single-Binary falls to 79%79\% and 84%84\%. The wider key coverage therefore mainly buys resistance to generalisation decay under accumulated interference: a 1010-point advantage at T=10T=10 and 5.55.5 points at T=100T=100. Locality is comparable between the two: from 100%100\% after a single edit it falls to about 6767–68%68\% at T=10T=10 for both methods and settles at 76%/74%76\%/74\% (Single/Multi) at T=25T=25 and 73.6%/72.7%73.6\%/72.7\% at T=100T=100, with Multi-Binary within 3.53.5 points of Single-Binary throughout. The stronger generalisation retention is thus not bought with additional interference on unrelated examples.

D.6 QAEdit: breakdown by target length

Table 16 breaks the LLaDA-8B source-prompt results of Table 4 down by the token length of the gold answer. Free-generation quality varies only mildly over 11–44 word targets (0.2240.224–0.2970.297 weighted) and is lowest on ≥5\geq\!5-word targets (0.1980.198), i.e. the editor degrades gracefully rather than failing outright on multi-token objects, but longer targets remain the harder case. This is consistent with the multi-token degradation reported by Park and Jo (2026), whose correction we compose with our view family in App. D.7.

D.7 Composing with decoding-state views: reproducing Park & Jo on QAEdit

App. A argues that the failure mode identified by Park and Jo (2026) (a value fitted on a fully masked target is not optimised for the partially revealed target states traversed during diffusion decoding) is orthogonal to the key-coverage failure mode this paper addresses, and that in the notation of §3.1.2 their correction is simply a further view type: a partial reveal of 𝒮o\mathcal{S}_{o} rather than an occlusion of 𝒮r\mathcal{S}_{r}. Because the two concern different axes of the same editor, the additional views can be supervised on the same shared value without any other change to equation 7. This appendix tests that composition empirically.

QAEdit is the setting in which the comparison is well posed. The reverse probes of §3.2.2 cannot discriminate a forward-only editor at all, but QAEdit scores freely decoded answers, which is exactly the regime the decoding-state correction targets: every answer token beyond the first is produced from a partially revealed target. We therefore reimplement the partial-reveal views on LLaDA-8B and add them to 𝒱\mathcal{V}, holding the view family, the key aggregation equation 8, the whitening equation 13, the write position and every hyperparameter of Table 7 fixed. The evaluation pool is unchanged from §3.2.3.

Findings.

The two corrections compose. On source prompts the weighted score rises from 0.2500.250 to 0.4300.430 and the fraction of previously wrong answers made at least partially correct from 32.5%32.5\% to 51.1%51.1\%, so the composed editor is at least partly right on a majority of the examples the unedited model got fully wrong; on paraphrased questions the corresponding figures are 0.187→0.3520.187\to 0.352 and 25.5%→43.7%25.5\%\to 43.7\%. Fully correct answers roughly double on both splits. The gain is obtained on top of the full view family of §3.1.2, with the key construction and the number of installed directions unchanged, so it is attributable to the view type Park and Jo (2026) contribute rather than to additional optimisation signal along an axis we already cover.

Table 18 locates that gain where the two-failure-mode reading predicts it. The multi-token degradation of Table 16 is largely removed: the ≥5\geq\!5-word bucket, the worst case for Multi-View at 0.1980.198, reaches 0.3000.300, and every multi-token bucket now scores above the best single-token result of the uncomposed editor (0.2970.297). What remains is a single step from one-word to multi-word targets (0.4340.434 vs. 0.3000.300–0.3200.320) rather than continued decay with length: across the 22–≥5\geq\!5 buckets the spread falls from 6.96.9 to 2.02.0 points. The component of the length effect that the decoding-state views remove is thus the component that accumulates with the number of revealed target tokens, as their diagnosis implies; the residual one-word advantage is not a decoding-trajectory effect and we do not account for it here.

Appendix E A Key-Space Account of Statement-Level Generalisation

The design principle of §3.1.1 (supervise the edit on views that span the region of key space the fact is queried from) can be made precise. We define generalisation as an objective over the conditionals a fact induces at deployment, note that under the rank-one update of equation 9 this objective is governed entirely by the trigger strength of equation 10, and show that (i) the expected trigger over a query family is maximised by the family’s mean key, with the single-view editor suffering a closed-form attenuation (Prop. 1); (ii) no single rank-one association serves both query directions, one per direction suffices, and reverse generalisation decomposes into a direction term and a within-direction coverage term (Prop. 2); (iii) the finite view family of §3.1.2 attains the population optimum up to a view-shift term controlled by sampling from the model’s own qtq_{t} and a sampling term decaying with the view budget (Prop. 3). The treatment is a first-order analysis of the editor’s linear algebra; its one modelling assumption is stated explicitly and is checkable against the measured triggers of §3.2.4.

E.1 Setup and notation

Masked-diffusion objective.

A masked DLM pθp_{\theta} is trained to reconstruct randomly hidden tokens. Given xx and a mask rate t∼𝒰⁡(0,1)t\!\sim\!\mathcal{U}(0,1), the corruption operator qtq_{t} replaces each token independently by [MASK] with probability tt, and the training loss is the (negative) ELBO

ℒELBO(x)=𝔼t∼𝒰⁡(0,1)𝔼x~∼qt(⋅∣x)[1t∑p:x~p=[MASK]−logpθ(xp∣x~)].\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}}(x)\;=\;\mathbb{E}_{t\sim\mathcal{U}(0,1)}\;\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{x}\sim q_{t}(\cdot\mid x)}\Big[\tfrac{1}{t}\!\!\sum_{p\,:\,\tilde{x}_{p}=\texttt{[MASK]}}\!\!-\log p_{\theta}\!\left(x_{p}\mid\tilde{x}\right)\Big]. (14)

Two features of equation 14 underlie the analysis below. Where an AR model is trained on p⁡(o∣s,r)p(o\mid s,r) alone, equation 14 trains the model on every conditional in which one subset of xx is visible and another is predicted, so the forward and reverse queries of Definition 2 are draws from the same family the model was trained on. And because the model is queried under qtq_{t} at decoding time as well, the keys an edit meets at test time come from partially masked inputs; this is why both the view family of §3.1.2 and the whitening covariance of equation 13 are drawn under qtq_{t}.

Editor notation.

Fix an edit (s,r,o)→(s,r,o∗)(s,r,o)\!\to\!(s,r,o^{\ast}) and an edit layer (suppressed throughout; the MEMIT spreading of equation 9 divides one residual across layers and changes nothing below). Let C≻0C\succ 0 be the regularised second moment of equation 13, estimated on keys of the corpus 𝒟\mathcal{D} under the masking distribution qtq_{t}; we write D~\tilde{D} for that key distribution and φ(k)=C−1/2k\varphi(k)=C^{-1/2}k for the whitened key, so that 𝔼D~​[φ⁡(k)​φ​(k)⊤]=I\mathbb{E}_{\tilde{D}}[\varphi(k)\varphi(k)^{\top}]=I up to the Tikhonov term. Let aa denote the aggregation key the update is written along (a=kavga=k_{\mathrm{avg}} in equation 8). In whitened coordinates equation 10 reads

αa​(k)=⟨φ⁡(a),φ⁡(k)⟩∥φ⁡(a)∥2,αa​(a)=1.\alpha_{a}(k)=\frac{\langle\varphi(a),\varphi(k)\rangle}{\lVert\varphi(a)\rVert^{2}},\qquad\alpha_{a}(a)=1. (15)
Definition 2 (Fact-query distribution).

At deployment the fact is interrogated through masked conditionals under the corruption qtq_{t} of equation 14: object-prediction queries with varying relation wording, context and mask pattern (forward, QfQ_{f}), and subject-prediction queries from the object side (reverse, QrQ_{r}). Model this as the mixture Q=πf​Qf+πr​QrQ=\pi_{f}Q_{f}+\pi_{r}Q_{r} with weights πf+πr=1\pi_{f}+\pi_{r}=1. Assumption 1 (Linear response).

Fix the installed value zz. For a query qq in direction dd, the editing effect Δ​logit​(q)\Delta\mathrm{logit}(q) of §3.2.4 (with the target subject in place of onewo_{\mathrm{new}} for reverse queries) satisfies Δ​logit​(q)=γd​αa​(κ⁡(q))\Delta\mathrm{logit}(q)=\gamma_{d}\,\alpha_{a}(\kappa(q)), where γd>0\gamma_{d}>0 if zz is adequate on QdQ_{d} (attains the stopping loss of equation 7 on that family) and γd≤0\gamma_{d}\leq 0 otherwise.
