E.4 Finite views, and why they are drawn from qtq_{t}

Let PVP_{V} denote the distribution over direction-dd views induced by the construction of §3.1.2 (occlusion ratio drawn from 𝒫ρ\mathcal{P}_{\rho}, occlusion pattern, context template), and write μPV=𝔼v∼PV​[φ⁡(k⁡(v))]\mu_{P_{V}}=\mathbb{E}_{v\sim P_{V}}[\varphi(k(v))] and ΣV\Sigma_{V} for the mean and covariance of the whitened view keys.

Proposition 3 (Approximate maximisation from finitely many views).

Let v1,…,vn​∼iid​PVv_{1},\dots,v_{n}\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}P_{V} and let a^\hat{a} be their aggregated key (equation 8; φ\varphi is linear, so φ⁡(a^)\varphi(\hat{a}) is the mean of the whitened view keys). For a failure probability δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) put η=(∥μPV−μd∥+tr⁡ΣV/(n​δ))/∥μd∥\eta=\big(\lVert\mu_{P_{V}}-\mu_{d}\rVert+\sqrt{\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{V}/(n\delta)}\big)/\lVert\mu_{d}\rVert. With probability ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta over the draw of the views,

Gd​(a^)≥1−η(1+η)2≥ 1−3​η.G_{d}(\hat{a})\;\geq\;\frac{1-\eta}{(1+\eta)^{2}}\;\geq\;1-3\eta. (19)
Proof.

φ⁡(a^)=μd+e\varphi(\hat{a})=\mu_{d}+e with e=(μPV−μd)+ξne=(\mu_{P_{V}}-\mu_{d})+\xi_{n}, where ξn\xi_{n} is the sampling deviation of the empirical mean, 𝔼​∥ξn∥2=tr⁡ΣV/n\mathbb{E}\lVert\xi_{n}\rVert^{2}=\operatorname{tr}\Sigma_{V}/n. Chebyshev gives ∥e∥≤η⁡∥μd∥\lVert e\rVert\leq\eta\lVert\mu_{d}\rVert w.p. ≥1−δ\geq 1-\delta, and Cauchy–Schwarz in equation 17 yields the first bound; (1−η)−(1−3​η)​(1+η)2=5​η2+3​η3≥0(1-\eta)-(1-3\eta)(1+\eta)^{2}=5\eta^{2}+3\eta^{3}\geq 0 gives the second. ∎

The bound separates two errors. The sampling term decays with the view budget nn. The view-shift term ∥μPV−μd∥\lVert\mu_{P_{V}}-\mu_{d}\rVert does not decay with nn: it depends only on which distribution the views are drawn from. Generating views with the model’s own qtq_{t} (the operator that defines the deployment conditionals in equation 14) and marginalising the occlusion ratio over 𝒫ρ\mathcal{P}_{\rho} ties PVP_{V} to QdQ_{d} structurally, without a paraphrase resource; Single-View is the degenerate case in which PVP_{V} is a point mass at the edit sentence, whose shift equals the full dispersion β​∥μ∥\beta\lVert\mu\rVert of Prop. 1(ii) and which no budget reduces. This is the reading of the budget-matched ablation (Tables 11–12): at fixed nn, changing the composition of the family changes μPV\mu_{P_{V}}, and nearly all of the gain moves with it.

E.5 Predictions and scope

The account predicts, and the paper confirms: (P1) forward-only editing leaves reverse metrics at baseline despite the reverse conditional being available (Prop. 2(i); Single-Forward, Table 3); (P2) reverse gains arrive in two separable steps (Remark 2; Table 3); (P3) at matched budget, gains track the composition of the view family, not its size (Prop. 3; Tables 11–12); (P4) widening the family leaves the unrelated-query trigger unchanged (Remark 1; α≈0.03\alpha\approx 0.03 in §3.2.4); (P5) paraphrase gains split into a small trigger and a large value component (Assumption 1(c); Fig. 4).

The analysis is idealised: Assumption 1 linearises a small rank-one update; ε,R,β\varepsilon,R,\beta and the view shift are measured, not derived from the architecture; the treatment is per-fact and does not model sequential interference (App. D.5) or the decoding-trajectory failure mode, which is orthogonal to the key-coverage axis (App. A, App. D.7). Within these limits, the view family is not an augmentation heuristic but a Monte-Carlo estimator of the two population directions, one per query direction, that maximise equation 16 under the editor’s own update rule.

Appendix F Evidence Retrieval: Benchmarks, Protocols and Controls

F.1 Controlled benchmark from PopQA facts

Corpus and queries.

The controlled benchmark is built from PopQA facts (Mallen et al., 2023) and is strictly balanced over five domains (Table 19). It contains 1,3821{,}382 entities and 5,5285{,}528 evidence cards over 1919 distinct relations (citizenship appears in both the person and the sports domain); every entity carries exactly the four relations of its domain. Each card states the subject first, then its relation and the source answer string(s), for example For “Film A”, the director is Person X. Ambiguous names are removed globally and the entity sets of different domains are disjoint. Each domain contributes 2020 validation and 6060 test entities, giving 3,6003{,}600 validation and 10,80010{,}800 test queries; each test domain has 720720 single-target, 720720 adjacent dual-target and 720720 crossed dual-target queries, so the five domains and three layouts are weighted equally. No example is filtered by whether a model answers it. Adjacent queries place each entity next to its relation clause (For “A”, identify the director; for “B”, identify the producer); crossed queries name both entities first and assign relations by reference (For “A” and “B”, identify the director for the former and the producer for the latter). Entity spans are recorded when rendering each template.

Readouts and baselines.

For subject retrieval, the vector for target jj is the hidden state at the last subject token (L0, plain input) or the mean over its subject span at the selected deeper layer under the retrieval prompt; each card is represented at its own subject span, and the branch-specific score is the cosine similarity between the two. Whole-query pooling averages the hidden states of the original input text, excluding chat wrappers, padding and representative-token suffixes. DiffRetriever uses its released zero-shot single-step encoding with four query and sixteen passage representations; PromptReps uses up to twenty sequential representative tokens on Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. Dense scoring uses normalized vectors with nonnegative MaxSim; hybrid scoring equally combines min–max-normalized dense and sparse scores. BM25 uses Porter stemming. One setting per method maximizes the validation mean of single R@1, adjacent All@2 and crossed All@2, and all settings are fixed before test evaluation.

Protocols.

In global search each subject branch ranks the full corpus; retrieval alternates between branches and removes duplicate cards until the total budget of two is met, with no entity-based candidate filter. Global pooling and the official retrievers return a single ranking. Single R@1 measures retrieval of the exact target card; dual All@2 measures whether both target cards occur within two retrieved cards. The entity-conditioned protocol gives every method the same visible entity spans and an exact unique-title linker: each target has four candidate cards (its four relations), and at budget two each entity receives one card, so the protocol isolates relation choice from entity coverage. Global methods reuse their scores within each candidate set; hybrid normalization and fusion are performed within it. Readout selection is repeated on validation under this protocol.

Findings.

On two-entity queries every single-vector method collapses in global search: the best adjacent and crossed All@2 among BM25, pooling, DiffRetriever and PromptReps are 3.063.06 and 2.502.50. Per-entity access states retrieve both cards for 38.2838.28–41.94%41.94\% of adjacent and 21.7821.78–38.08%38.08\% of crossed queries from the deeper layers, and for 13.3213.32–24.44%24.44\% and 9.449.44–13.33%13.33\% from the first block. The entity-conditioned protocol, which removes entity coverage as a factor, leaves the ordering unchanged: subject L31 reaches 41.94/38.0841.94/38.08 against at most 16.35/16.2616.35/16.26 for the baselines, so the advantage lies in relation choice within an entity’s cards, not in finding the entity. Single-entity search over the full corpus is where the representative-token and lexical retrievers are strongest (DiffRetriever hybrid 97.6997.69, BM25 92.8292.82, against 89.0889.08 for subject L31); the deeper readouts also lead the first-block readout there, in contrast to the natural setting of App. F.2, where the candidate set is a question’s own context and the first-block state is the best allocator.

F.2 Natural comparison-question RAG

We evaluate multi-entity evidence retrieval and answer generation on the comparison subsets of HotpotQA and 2WikiMultiHopQA. A question is retained when its official ten-paragraph distractor context provides two unambiguous entity mentions and two valid gold evidence groups. We reserve 100 questions from each dataset for validation and evaluate on all remaining eligible questions: 1,296 from HotpotQA and 2,933 from 2WikiMultiHopQA. One additional 2Wiki question is excluded because its annotated supporting-sentence index is outside the corresponding paragraph. The resulting frozen corpus contains 106,329 unique Wikipedia sentences, each prefixed with its paragraph title. For every question, a retriever ranks the sentences in its official distractor context and returns two total sentences. These sentences are placed in an identical prompt for a frozen Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct reader, which generates a short answer with greedy decoding.

We compare BM25, whole-query pooling, PromptReps, the released dense and hybrid DiffRetriever variants, and subject-state retrieval on Dream-7B and LLaDA-8B. Dream and LLaDA DiffRetriever use four query and sixteen passage representations; Qwen PromptReps uses twenty of each. L0 subject retrieval reads the last subject token from the plain input. The deeper subject variants read the mean subject state at Dream L27 or LLaDA L31 under the retrieval prompt. For a two-entity question, subject retrieval forms one ranking per entity, alternates between the two rankings, and removes duplicate sentences until the shared budget of two is filled. All configurations are fixed before test evaluation. Support R@2 measures recall over annotated supporting sentences, while Both@2 measures whether the retrieved pair covers both gold evidence titles. End-to-end answer quality is reported with normalized exact match and token F1. Latency is the median per-query time from question to retrieved evidence, excluding answer generation, at batch size 1 with resident model and index; neural methods run on one H200 and BM25 on the host CPU.

Dream L0 provides the strongest evidence retrieval on both datasets (Table 20). Its Both@2 exceeds Dream DiffRetriever hybrid by 25.54 points on HotpotQA (paired 95% CI [22.30,28.78][22.30,28.78]) and by 28.37 points on 2WikiMultiHopQA ([26.49,30.24][26.49,30.24]). The improved evidence allocation raises answer F1 by 6.71 points ([4.02,9.48][4.02,9.48]) and 19.14 points ([17.12,21.22][17.12,21.22]), respectively. Relative to BM25, Dream L0 improves Both@2 by 16.67 points on HotpotQA and 10.44 points on 2Wiki, together with EM gains of 5.87 and 3.99 points. On HotpotQA, the LLaDA L31 subject state gives the strongest final answers, reaching 61.34 EM and 69.81 F1; on 2Wiki, Dream L0 is the strongest non-oracle method on all four metrics. Entity-specific subject states thus allocate a fixed retrieval budget across the two targets of a natural comparison question, and the improvement carries through to the generated answer.

F.3 Causal intervention and matching controls

The interventions in this subsection use Dream-7B-Instruct and the earlier, film-only version of the controlled benchmark (3,7453{,}745 cards, 5,1965{,}196 queries in the same single, adjacent and crossed layouts).

Summary.

The dependence on relation fusion is causal. On Dream, we subtract the first attention layer’s relation-token value messages at the subject positions, keeping all other attention weights and the document index fixed. Within-entity relation R@1 falls to the 25%25\% four-choice chance level in all three layouts (→27.154.3\!\to\!27.1 single, →25.359.1\!\to\!25.3 adjacent, →25.442.5\!\to\!25.4 crossed), while mass-matched and norm-matched random messages leave it at the clean level (Fig. 12; Holm-adjusted p≃0.0003p\simeq 0.0003 in each layout), and entity identification stays at 100%100\%. The same loss appears at the L1 MLP key, the representation that §2 identified as the lookup key (Table 21). Replacing the removed message with a norm-matched message of a different relation from the same entity redirects retrieval toward that relation: donor-relation selection rises from 14.89%14.89\% to 56.38%56.38\% on single queries and from 33.83%33.83\% to 57.57%57.57\% on adjacent queries. Early access states thus carry the relation information that selects evidence, and reading them is the counterpart of the write in §3: the layer-00 routing that an edit must cover is what a retrieval vector taken from the state already contains.

Protocol.

The causal experiment uses plain queries in Dream Instruct. We recompute queries and all document states in float32, keep the document index fixed, and intervene only on query-side L0 attention. For subject position ii and relation-token set RR, let

mR​(i)=WO​concath​[∑t∈Rαi​th​vth].m_{R}(i)=W_{O}\operatorname{concat}_{h}\left[\sum_{t\in R}\alpha^{h}_{it}v^{h}_{t}\right]. (20)

We subtract mR​(i)m_{R}(i) from the attention output at every token in each subject span. RR includes the visible relation-word tokens from all target clauses in the query. Other attention weights remain unchanged: there is no softmax renormalization. We read the resulting L0 residual, L2 residual, and actual input to the L1 MLP down-projection (the MLP key). These have dimensions 3,584, 3,584, and 18,944, respectively. The clean float32 global scores differ from the original bfloat16 scores by at most 0.87 percentage points; every causal contrast uses the same float32 computation.

The thirteen conditions comprise clean input; relation-message removal; three native random-message removals; three exact-mass random-message controls; a residual-norm-matched random control; clean relation add-back; wrong-relation add-back; former/latter-message removal; and all non-subject-template-message removal. Random token sets exclude subject, relation, reference, and special tokens. For each seed, subject position, and attention head, we sample 256 same-cardinality subsets and select the closest attention-mass match without retrieval scores or correctness labels.

The native random subsets have mean relative mass errors of 32.39%, 32.68%, and 32.51%. The exact controls reweight each selected set to the relation mass before output projection, achieving maximum effective relative errors below 2.4×10−72.4\times 10^{-7}. Their maximum scaling factor is 1.97×1071.97\times 10^{7}: these are reweighted message interventions rather than native-edge deletions. Independently, the norm control scales a random projected message to ‖mR​(i)‖2\|m_{R}(i)\|_{2}, matching the residual perturbation size with relative error below 1.67×10−71.67\times 10^{-7}. We report both control families because they constrain different aspects of the intervention.

Content transfer and reference binding.

The donor uses the same entity and template with a different requested relation. Single-target donors cycle to another relation; dual-target donors swap the two relations while preserving both entities and the word bag. We replace mR​(i)m_{R}(i) by the donor’s relation contribution, aligned to the same subject tokens and scaled to its original norm. Wrong-relation selection increases by 41.49 points on single queries (95% CI [38.56,44.43][38.56,44.43]) and 23.74 points on adjacent queries ([20.75,26.91][20.75,26.91]). In crossed queries it decreases by 5.45 points ([−7.16,−3.79][-7.16,-3.79]): clean states already favor the donor relation (47.95%) over the intended relation (42.53%). After transfer, correct-relation accuracy rises to 48.34%. Relation availability and reference binding are therefore empirically separable. Removing the messages from former/latter tokens has a small effect on this L0 subject readout; directly reading or patching those tokens is a separate localization experiment.

Inference and implementation checks.

The prespecified primary contrast is the mean of the three exact-mass controls minus relation removal in L0 relation R@1, separately for each layout. Differences are 30.54, 34.25, and 16.62 points, with 95% paired cluster-bootstrap intervals [28.49,32.53][28.49,32.53], [32.17,36.39][32.17,36.39], and [15.30,17.88][15.30,17.88]. We use 10,000 bootstrap and sign-flip draws; Holm correction across the three primary tests gives p≃0.00030p\simeq 0.00030 for each. Norm-matched contrasts have the same direction. Global entity identification remains 100% for clean and relation removal; the paired interval [0,0][0,0] lies inside the fixed ±2\pm 2-point equivalence margin. This is preservation of the measured identification endpoint at ceiling, rather than identity of the full entity representation.

Clean-message add-back restores all saved readouts exactly, serving as an algebraic implementation check. Reconstructed attention contributions match native scaled-dot-product attention with maximum relative error 6.08×10−56.08\times 10^{-5}. A six-query preflight verifies every non-subject L0 position is unchanged; the full run saves subject readouts only. The audit checks all 77 entity-conditioned result rows, all 5,196 causal queries at three readouts, donor alignment, finite features, validation selections, metric aggregation, and code/data hashes. The follow-up protocol was frozen before these evaluations and reuses the already-inspected main-table test set. The resulting claim concerns frozen-model factual evidence selection and its causal dependence on early relation messages; answer generation and latency are reported in App. F.2.

Appendix G Limitations

We list the limitations we consider most material, in rough order of how much they constrain the claims of the paper.

Free-generation transfer is improved, not solved.

The QAEdit results of §3.2.3 show that Multi-View produces a clear improvement in free generation after a statement-only edit: 44.6%44.6\% and 32.5%32.5\% of previously wrong answers become at least partially correct. We want to be explicit that this is not the same as having solved statement-to-question transfer. In absolute terms the weighted scores are 0.3420.342 (Dream) and 0.2500.250 (LLaDA); fully correct answers are 23.8%23.8\% and 17.6%17.6\%; and 55.4%55.4\% and 67.5%67.5\% of edits are still answered wrongly. On a paraphrased question (the Gen. split) the numbers fall further. A user who edits a fact by stating it and then asks about it in natural question form should therefore still expect the edited model to be wrong more often than right. The contribution here is a measurable step on a metric where AR editors have been brittle, not a deployable level of reliability.

The edit specification is structured.

Although we describe the input as a declarative statement, the current construction assumes identifiable subject, relation, and object spans. Benchmarks such as CounterFact and BAKE provide this structure naturally, whereas arbitrary user statements may contain multiple predicates, qualifiers, or non-contiguous relations. Extending statement-level editing to such inputs requires a mechanism for proposition decomposition and span discovery, which is outside the scope of the present editor.

Retrieval assumes identifiable entity spans and two-entity questions.

Both settings provide the entity spans: matched paragraph titles in the natural setting, templated spans in the controlled benchmark. Questions with more than two entities, implicit or nested mentions, or spans that must be detected first are untested, and the natural setting ranks within a question’s official distractor context rather than an open corpus.

Global single-entity search favours representative-token and lexical retrievers.

On the controlled benchmark, DiffRetriever hybrid and BM25 reach 97.7%97.7\% and 92.8%92.8\% single R@1 against 89.1%89.1\% for the best access-state readout (Table 5). The access state’s advantage is in allocating evidence across entities; there the deeper readouts help in global search and cost a full forward pass, while the first-block readout is best where the candidate set is a question’s own context.
